annotations.title: Starlink satellites: Facts, tracking and impact on astronomy

content.text:
**Do you mean the first artificial satellite vs a modern/latest type of satellite?** If so, here’s a simple comparison:

| Feature | **First satellite: Sputnik 1** | **Modern/latest satellites** |
|---|---|---|
| Launched | **October 4, 1957** | New satellites are launched almost weekly/monthly |
| Country/company | Soviet Union | Governments and private companies: SpaceX, NASA, ESA, China, Amazon, etc. |
| Size | About **58 cm** diameter — beach-ball sized | From tiny CubeSats to large internet/spy/weather satellites |
| Mass | **83.6 kg** | Often hundreds to thousands of kg; Starlink V2 Mini is about **800 kg** |
| Power | Batteries only | Solar panels + batteries |
| Main job | Sent simple radio “beeps” | Internet, GPS, weather, Earth imaging, military, science, communications |
| Communication | Basic radio signal | High-speed data, laser links, phased-array antennas |
| Lifespan | About **3 months in orbit** | Often 5–15+ years, depending on mission |
| Technology level | Very simple metal sphere with antennas | Computers, sensors, cameras, propulsion, AI-assisted operations |
| Impact | Started the **Space Age** | Supports daily life: navigation, phones, banking, weather forecasts, internet |

Sputnik 1 was the **world’s first artificial satellite**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**. NASA describes it as about the size of a beach ball, weighing **83.6 kg**, and orbiting Earth every **98 minutes**. ([nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/sputnik.html?utm_source=openai))

For a “latest” example, modern Starlink V2 Mini satellites are much larger and more capable, using advanced antennas and high-capacity communications; they are designed to provide far more internet capacity than earlier satellites. ([space.com](https://www.space.com/spacex-starlink-satellites.html?utm_source=openai))

**In short:** Sputnik 1 proved humans could put an object in orbit. Modern satellites are working machines that provide internet, navigation, weather data, surveillance, and science services every day.
